newsitem.title: USA: IBM to unveil new mainframes, Amdahl attacks.
newsitem.headline: IBM to unveil new mainframes, Amdahl attacks.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. on Monday will unveil a much-anticipated upgrade to its microprocessor-based mainframe family with models that finally match the power of its older mainframe line.

Wall Street and IBM customers have been waiting for this fourth generation model, called the G4, because it is expected to match the processing power of IBM's older bipolar mainframe models, which IBM no longer manufactures.
In its first quarter, IBM's mainframe revenues declined sharply, in part due to delays in purchases as customers waited for the new, faster models.

While IBM's mainframe hardware revenues are an increasingly smaller portion of the computer giant's total revenue, mainframes are still important to IBM. These big systems, which still run many corporations around the world, also drive sales of IBM's mainframe software, storage and maintenance services.
"Clearly there is some anticipation," said Linda Sanford, general manager of IBM's System/390 mainframe line. "We do have very good customer excitement about this product."
IBM said it has placed 10 systems in an "early ship" programme and will continue to ship the systems in the month of June.

The new G4 mainframe has the processing power of about 63 million instructions per second, or MIPS, which is the fastest model in this lower-cost mainframe line. The system can hold as many as 10 processors, for a total processing power of 405 MIPS.

In 1993 IBM introduced an entirely new mainframe generation using lower-cost microprocessor technology called CMOS, for complementary metal oxide semiconductor. This new generation is cheaper to develop because it uses off-the-shelf instead of customised parts and it is less expensive for companies to operate and maintain because the system takes up less floor space and consumes less power.
The CMOS mainframes have been successful in helping keep IBM's once-moribund mainframe business alive.
"It is a necessary announcement for the health of the company," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst. "People have been waiting for it."
But the steep pricing competition in the business continues, and one of IBM's two big rivals, Amdahl Corp., is hoping to steal some of IBM's thunder with announcements of its own.

Amdahl on Monday will announce an upgrade path for its current family of CMOS mainframes, called the Millennium. Amdahl said that next March it will offer customers systems with processors of 75 MIPS that can go up to 12 processors for a total processing capability of 650 MIPS.

"We want our customers to know what our products will look like as they make the transition from bipolar to CMOS," said Ali Jenab, vice president of worldwide processor marketing at Amdahl, based in Sunnyvale, Calif.
Analysts said Amdahl hopes its "roadmap" announcement will lead some mainframe customers to wait for Amdahl's faster processing capability instead of buying IBM's new machines.
"Obviously, that is what they are hoping. But I find it very hard to believe they will do that," Jones said. "By next March, IBM could have an equivalent machine if they really want to."

"There is this game of leapfrog that goes on," said Mike Kahn, chairman of the Clipper Group in Wellesley, Mass. "It becomes a question of delivery schedule. When can I get it and how much do I have to pay for it?"

IBM, for its part, said it is improving its mainframe performance in very rapid cycles of about 12 to 18 months, compared with its old bipolar upgrades, which took about three to five years to develop performance improvements.

"We are leading the charge here as it relates to CMOS technology," Sanford said. "MIPS aren't everything. Customers are looking to solve business problems and they look to us to deliver a solution." She declined to make any projections, but Jones estimates that IBM will unveil its fifth-generation system, the G5, at 80-90 MIPS, in the June or September quarter of 1998.

IBM is also upgrading its mainframe operating system, called OS/390, to make it even more Internet-ready so that IBM's mainframes can also run applications developed in Java, Sun Microsystems Inc.'s programming language, which is widely used for Internet applications. It also has added cryptography to both hardware and software, for securing transactions over networks.

IBM still dominates the mainframe market, with about an 80 percent share. Amdahl, which has been losing market share over the last year or so, said it hopes to increase its current 10 percent share to between 15 to 20 percent. The third player in the market is Hitachi Data Systems, a unit of Hitachi Ltd.

Gary Helmig, a SoundView Financial analyst, said the G4 announcement should be positively received by investors as well, citing rumours in March that the G4 mainframe would not be introduced until September or October.
"These machines are not only getting announced next week, they will be shipping," Helmig said.

Jones estimates that IBM's System/390, with the new models, will generate about $275 million in revenues in IBM's second quarter. That should account for about 35 percent of his total estimate of mainframe hardware revenue in 1997.

IBM declined to disclosed pricing of the new models, saying prices are negotiated with customers. Amdahl said its current 400 and 500 Series range in price from about $600,000 up to $3 million and its new 75 MIP model may range in price from about $2 million up to $5 million for a 12-way model.
